newsitem.title: UK: C&W can gain by switching alliances - analysts.
newsitem.headline: C&W can gain by switching alliances - analysts.

text.p: Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc has plenty to gain if it turns its back on partners in a German telecommunications alliance to fall in with weightier telecoms players in a major global partnership, analysts said on Monday.

But they warned the company risks short-term share weakness if it abandons German utilities Veba AG and RWE AG to swim with bigger fish. Veba has a 10.5-percent stake in C&W and could sell if spurned by the British group.
C&W and Veba formed a strategic alliance, called Vebacom, in 1995. Last year, the firms agreed to bring RWE into the alliance and final contracts were drawn up two weeks ago.
But C&W has not yet signed the deal -- and while the group declined to comment on Monday , newspapers have speculated that the alliance is on the rocks.
If Britain's second biggest telecoms operator pulls out of this German deal, a question mark may also hang over a similar agreement it has with Veba in France, analysts noted.

An RWE official said on Saturday that C&W was exploring the possibility of joining Global One, a partnership of Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint Corp of the U.S. C&W has declined to comment, repeating only its stock phrase -- that it talks to everyone all the time.
A deal with C&W would be a good coup for Global One as it would give it access to lucrative Asian and British markets.
However, analysts say C&W must choose between sealing the German alliance and joining Global One as the two groups would go head to head in the German market.
"It's reasonable to assume that something like a link-up with Global One will happen and on balance we think it would be a net positive for C&W," Nikko Europe analyst Dennis Exton said.
He said C&W chief executive Richard Brown, a former Sprint executive, was known to favour a focus on the U.S. and Asia rather than Europe.

"Brown is more concerned about C&W having a sensible business strategy vis-a-vis Europe and the U.S. rather than Europe," Exton said. "Europe is rather sclerotic and there are lots of minefields as it moves through privatisation and liberalisation to full competition."
John Tysoe, analyst at brokers SocGen, agreed a deal with Global One looked increasingly likely. "It would undoubtedly be more beneficial than going in with Vebacom," he said.
Analysts also noted that abandoning the German deal could help C&W's shares -- although a sale by Veba of its 10.5 percent stake could also weaken the stock in the near-term.
"In the short-term...C&W would no longer have to consolidate 50 million pounds ($80.17 million) worth of losses, and something like two pence a share could be saved," Tysoe said.
Exton noted that C&W would also receive a capital gain of around 600 million pounds if it sold its stake in E-Plus, the German mobile telephone operator in which Veba has an interest.
James Golob, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said because of C&W's relatively small size, an equal partnership in Global One "would not be remotely achievable".

But analysts agreed that C&W would be extremely attractive to Global One. "If C&W were to join it would give Global One direct access into China through Hong Kong, as well as access to the UK," Exton said.

C&W's jewel is its lucrative 57.5 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications. It also has a 17 percent stake in the second-largest carrier in Japan, the world's second-biggest telecoms market, and a very attractive base in Britain, which may become the hub for most U.S.-Europe traffic.

Global One is one of three major global groups. The others are Concert, which comprises British Telecommunications and MCI Communications, and World Partners/Unisource, a loosely-knit group dreamt up by U.S. phone giant AT&T.
Attempts by BT to link up with Japan's telecoms titan Nippon Telegraph and Telephone has thrown down the gauntlet to rival global groups trying to get into Asia. ($1=.6237 Pound)
